nameStory: The humped bladderwort gets its name from the tiny inflated bladders that dot its underwater stems, which look like little humps when viewed closely. These bladders aren't just for show - they're actually miniature traps that snap shut to catch tiny water creatures! It's also called floating bladderwort because it forms mats that drift freely in the water.
description: Humped bladderwort is a fascinating carnivorous aquatic plant that forms thin, floating mats on the water's surface. This small plant has thread-like underwater stems dotted with microscopic trap bladders and produces tiny yellow flowers that poke above the water. The entire plant is usually only a few inches across, creating delicate green carpets that drift with the current in ponds and slow-moving streams.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms thin, mat-like carpets that float freely on the water surface, feeling delicate and almost feathery when you gently lift a section

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers on thin stalks that emerge above the water surface, each about the size of a pencil eraser

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thread-like underwater stems and leaves create a fine, almost hair-like texture when touched gently in the water

idTips.label: Bladders
idTips.description: Microscopic clear bladders dot the underwater portions - you'll need a magnifying glass to see these tiny traps clearly

habitat: Look for humped bladderwort in quiet, shallow waters of ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It prefers nutrient-poor to moderately rich waters and is often found mixed with other aquatic plants in areas with little current. You might spot it in beaver ponds, shallow lake edges, or marshy areas where the water stays relatively still.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water warms, with fresh green mats starting to form and spread across the water surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and flowering season - look for the tiny yellow flowers rising above the floating mats from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Mats may persist into early fall but become less noticeable as flowers fade and growth slows with cooling water temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back or goes dormant, with specialized winter buds sinking to the bottom to survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: Despite being a tiny aquatic plant, humped bladderwort has one of the most compact genomes ever discovered in plants - it's packed an entire plant's worth of genetic information into a space smaller than many single-celled organisms use!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other small floating aquatic plants like duckweeds, but bladderworts have thread-like underwater parts (duckweeds have simple roots) and produce small yellow flowers on stalks (duckweeds have tiny inconspicuous flowers). Remember: if it has delicate underwater "threads" and yellow flowers, think bladderwort.
contextualKnowledge: Many people are surprised to learn that some plants can be carnivorous! Bladderworts represent one of the most sophisticated plant trapping mechanisms in nature, using suction to capture prey faster than the blink of an eye - though you need specialized equipment to actually see this happen.
compareHints: Humped bladderwort is much smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort, forming thin surface mats rather than robust underwater colonies. Unlike purple bladderwort which has wheel-like floating structures, humped bladderwort creates simple thread-like mats. It's distinguished from horned bladderwort by its aquatic (not terrestrial) habitat and floating growth pattern.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horned bladderwort stands out from its many bladderwort relatives by having the most prominent horn-like spur and by growing in terrestrial or semi-aquatic conditions rather than fully underwater.
Small swollen bladderwort is smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort and lacks the large inflated floats of swollen bladderwort.
Among New England's bladderworts, purple bladderwort is unique for its purple flowers – most others have yellow blooms.
Common bladderwort is the largest and most robust of New England's bladderworts, with the biggest flowers and most substantial underwater growth.
Swollen bladderwort is the largest of New England's aquatic bladderworts and the only one with truly prominent inflated stems that feel spongy to the touch.
Intermediate bladderwort differs from common bladderwort by having fewer, slightly smaller flowers and more delicate overall appearance.
Northeastern bladderwort is distinguished from other New England bladderworts by its lavender-purple flowers and preference for very shallow water or bog margins.

Hidden-fruit Bladderwort is unique among New England's bladderworts for keeping its flowers at or below the water surface, while most relatives like Common and Purple Bladderwort hold their blooms well above water on conspicuous stalks.
Lesser bladderwort is distinguished from common bladderwort by its much smaller size and more delicate appearance overall.
Among New England's bladderworts, zigzag bladderwort is unique for its terrestrial zigzag growth habit - most other bladderworts either float in water or grow upright from water.
Distinguished from common bladderwort by much finer, more delicate underwater stems and smaller overall size.
